The free introduction to the Wyrd Mandala at /learn/mandala: what the instrument is, its two rotors, its rings from the centre out, the two decks, the Asura voids (what they are, their spacing, their names, with a table of all thirty-six), how to read a station's record, three things to try, and the outline of the paid course (Learning the Mandala). The course itself is the paid teaching and stays off this page; only its module titles and one line each are shown here.
LEDE: The Wyrd Mandala is a study wheel: two zodiacs turning against each other, with the twenty-seven mansions, the hundred and eight padas, two decks of cards and the Asura voids laid on them. It needs no birth data. You read it directly, one station at a time, and lay your own chart on it when you want to.
ROTORS: The inner rings are sidereal: the zodiac measured from the stars. The outer rings are tropical: the zodiac measured from the spring equinox. The wheel opens at 0° sidereal Aries, the first pada of Ashwini, because the sidereal ring is where things come from: the stars. The tropical ring is where they land, in the seasons.

The two zeros stand about 24° apart in 2026, and the gap widens by a degree in roughly 72 years. That gap is the ayanamsa. On the wheel it is the distance the outer ring has turned, and the year slider turns it, from 285, when the two zodiacs met, to 2700.
RINGS: The bindu at the centre. The cross of the four cardinal sign starts, each a vargottama station. The triangle at 0°, 120° and 240°: the only three places where a sign boundary and a mansion boundary fall together. The Fool stands here, at the gate.
Twelve signs of 30°, each carrying its trump from the Buddhist deck.
The twenty-seven nakshatras of 13°20′, each with its number and its ruling planet.

A hundred and eight quarters of 3°20′: the stations of the wheel. A small ring marks a vargottama pada, whose navamsa repeats its own sign. The dark padas are the Asura voids. The dashed lines carry the sign boundaries through, so you can see where the signs and the mansions part company.
One card for every station: the minor card of its decan, read on the sidereal ring.
The thirty-six decans of the tropical ring, each with its minor card, turned by the ayanamsa.
Twelve signs measured from the equinox, each carrying its Nordic trump. The dashed equinox line marks 0° tropical Aries.
DECKS: The Buddhist deck belongs to the sidereal ring and the Nordic deck to the tropical. Both read the same thirty-six decans, so every station holds a card in each: where it comes from, and where it lands.

Because the tropical ring is turned by the ayanamsa, a pada can straddle two Nordic decans, and then it carries both cards. The trumps sit by sign, one in each deck. Seven more trumps of the Nordic deck stand outside the rim, each at its planet's exaltation on the tropical ring: the Sun at 19° Aries, the High Priestess (the Moon) at 3° Taurus, the Magician (Mercury) at 15° Virgo, the Empress (Venus) at 27° Pisces, the Tower (Mars) at 28° Capricorn, the Wheel (Jupiter) at 15° Cancer, the World (Saturn) at 21° Libra. The Fool belongs to no sign and no decan. It stands at the gate, 0° sidereal Aries, where the Buddhist ring begins.
VOIDS: In the oldest hymns asura is a title, not an enemy. The Rigveda calls Varuna, Mitra and Agni asura: lords, holders of power. From the Brahmanas on, the word turns. The asuras become the elder children of Prajapati and the devas the younger (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.3.1), and the two sides contest the worlds. The Puranas sort them by their mothers: the Daityas born of Diti, the Danavas born of Danu. Buddhist cosmology keeps them as a realm of their own, beneath Mount Sumeru, at war with the gods of the Thirty-Three above.

Both traditions put them underneath. The Vishnu Purana lays seven underworlds below the earth, the patalas, and gives them to the Daityas, the Danavas and the nagas. In the Bhagavata, Vamana sends Bali down to one of them, Sutala, after his three strides. That is why the voids are the tunnels: passages beneath the wheel.

The word is borrowed from Kenneth Grant, whose tunnels of Set run behind the paths of the Qabalistic Tree (Nightside of Eden, 1977). The voids take the image and not the lineage. They are not Grant's tunnels and claim no descent from them.

On the wheel the voids are this system's construction. Thirty-six of the hundred and eight padas are voids, three in every sign: the fourth, the seventh and the ninth pada of each sidereal sign. So the spacing runs three, two, four and repeats every 30°, and every sign closes on a void. In a station's record, the void is named after the cards.

Because the pattern repeats sign by sign, it falls in step with the mansions. The signs of each element close in the three mansions of one planet: the fire signs in the Sun's (Krittika, Uttara Phalguni, Uttara Ashadha), the earth signs in Mars's (Mrigashira, Chitra, Dhanishta), the air signs in Jupiter's (Punarvasu, Vishakha, Purva Bhadrapada) and the water signs in Mercury's (Ashlesha, Jyeshtha, Revati), where the closing voids sit in the three gandanta knots. Every void has another directly across the wheel, and one at each trine.

The names are the asuras of the Vedas, the epics and the Puranas. Vritra, Namuci and Swarbhanu, who darkened the sun, come from the Rigveda. Madhu and Kaitabha, Mahishasura, Sumbha and Nisumbha come from the Devi Mahatmya. Hiranyakashipu, his son Prahlada, Prahlada's grandson Bali and Bali's son Bana are one line. Tarakaksha and Vidyunmali are lords of Tripura, the three cities. A few are this system's compounds: Rahu-Asura and Ketu-Asura, Diti-Mula, Danu-Garbha, Maya-Vijnana and Hayagriva-Asura.

The void at station 90 is Narakasura. He is the son of the Earth, Bhumi, and so is called Bhauma, the earth-born, which is also a name of Mars. Naraka is the name of the hells (Bhagavata Purana 10.59; Vishnu Purana 5.29). Krishna kills him, and the day is kept as Naraka Chaturdashi, in the days of Diwali. His void is Dhanishta's second pada, the last of sidereal Capricorn, where Mars is exalted at its deepest, 28° Capricorn. Across the wheel, Simhika's void at station 36 holds Mars's deepest fall, 28° Cancer. The other two earth signs close on Swarbhanu (18) and Danu-Garbha (54), in Mars's other two mansions.
STATION: Tap a station and its record opens. Read it from the inside out: the mansion and its pada, the station's place on both rotors, its two cards with their trumps, its void if it has one, and then its correspondences.

The correspondences are lenses on the one station: the two rotors, the mansion, the planets and their rulership, the runes, colour, numerology, sound, Human Design on the tropical ring, the I Ching, the chakras and the Planetary Ladder, the tattvas, anatomy, the harmonic relationships and the mythological structures. None of them is the source of another. Each is a way of looking at the same arc of sky.
TRY_INTRO: Three things to try with the Mandala open beside this page.
TRY: Read its mansion, Ashwini, then its two cards: the Buddhist card of where it comes from and the Nordic card of where it lands. Then the Fool, at the gate.
Drag the year slider back to 285 and watch the outer ring turn until the two zeros meet. Then bring it forward to today and see how far the receiving ring has travelled.
Cast your chart and open the Mandala from it. Your planets stand at their stations. Open the station your Moon stands on and read it from the inside out.
COURSE_INTRO: Learning the Mandala is the course that teaches the reading itself: how a station speaks through its rings, how the two rotors and their decks answer each other, and how to read your own chart on the wheel. It will be sold on its own, apart from The Wyrd Reading, and included for the Order.
